slides.title: Pax Silica: Yes, No, or Conditions?

blocks.text: The Philippines joined a US-led AI supply-chain initiative. The real question is what participation must deliver—and what it must protect.
Critical minerals and materials feed semiconductor manufacturing.
Chips, energy, and advanced computing infrastructure support AI.

slides.title: The opportunity: move up the chain

blocks.text: Build local processing, technical skills, and supplier capacity.
Turn Philippine mineral and geographic advantages into lasting capability.

slides.title: The cost of a blank cheque

blocks.text: Water and power demand could compete with local needs.

slides.title: Neither slogan answers the hard question

blocks.text: Rejecting the initiative does not build a local chip industry. Joining does not guarantee jobs, technology transfer, or community protections.
Continue only with public terms, independent environmental review, and meaningful local and Indigenous consultation.
Require measurable local hiring, training, supplier participation, Philippine regulatory authority, and public progress reporting.
US-led partnerships promise access to advanced chips, investment, and trusted supply chains.
China-led alternatives compete on cost, openness, and access to a different technology ecosystem.
Some countries try to work with both. The Philippines should protect room to maneuver.
Publish land, lease, and governance terms before major commitments.
Disclose independent water, energy, and environmental assessments; consult affected communities.
Track local value added, skilled jobs, technology transfer, and compliance in public.
